newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan nuclear plant shutdown fuels safety demands.
newsitem.headline: Japan nuclear plant shutdown fuels safety demands.

text.p: The shutdown this week of another Japanese nuclear plant because of a brief radiation scare has added fuel to demands for a major overhaul of safety standards in the country's crucial atomic power industry.

The demands, both from within and outside government, extend even to calls for a reappraisal of energy-starved Japan's plans to make nuclear power the country's main energy source in the 21st century.
A string of accidents since the end of 1995, made worse either by efforts to cover up their seriousness or by failure to even report them, has put the nuclear industry under the microscope.
In a sign of how intense public scrutiny has become, the operator of one nuclear power plant on Wednesday swiftly reported a harmless fire in a toilet, lest it be accused of a new cover-up.
In the latest significant accident, Tokyo Electric Power Co (TEPCO) halted operations on Tuesday at a nuclear reactor after a rise in radioactivity levels in exhaust gas at the plant.
TEPCO officials said the brief rise in radiation was caused by a pin-sized hole in the metal cover of a nuclear fuel rod in the reactor.
They said no evacuation was needed and the plant was expected to reopen in about three weeks.

But after Japan's worst-ever nuclear accident last month, when 37 workers were exposed to low-level radiation at the country's only nuclear fuel reprocessing plant, Tuesday's plant shutdown gave new impetus for demands for reform.
"The accidents may affect plans to build more nuclear power plants in general," said Kazuya Fujime, a senior researcher at the Institute of Energy Economics.

Fujime, a supporter of nuclear power because of Japan's lack of oil, believes the bad luck -- or bad management -- dogging the industry at present will only delay, not end plans for atomic fuel to be the country's main fuel resource.
"The option of keeping the nuclear power programme going will probably remain but with a revision of time targets," he told Reuters.
Under the plan, Japan aims to boost electricity output from nuclear plants to 42 percent of total power needs by 2010 from the present 33 percent.
Before the end of the century, it hopes nuclear power will account for more than half of the country's energy needs.
Toshihiro Ichikawa, professor of physics at Tokyo's Meiji University, described nuclear power as a "necessary evil" but said the time had come to review energy policies.

"Regarding the nation's nuclear development programme, the Japanese government had never seriously reviewed the plan despite rapid developments since the programme was first outlined 30 some years ago," Ichikawa said.
"The programme was built on technology and socio-political circumstances of the time, and I think the public will agree with me that things have changed considerably since then," he added.

Most of the criticism has been directed at the government's own Power Reactor and Nuclear Fuel Development Corp (PNC), which was established in 1967 to carry out research, operate nuclear plants, recycle nuclear material and help Japan achieve energy self-sufficiency through nuclear power.

After recent revelations of lax safety and cover-ups in reporting the seriousness of accidents, there has been a chorus of calls for the PNC to either be completely privatised or be allowed only to carry out key research work.
"The government rarely changes its programmes and goals once they're established, but the PNC case is a good opportunity to force the government to review its policies," Ichikawa said.
